claims.text: Pirate measures application-layer response latency (time from request to last byte received) by observing only client-to-server packets at a load balancer, even with encrypted QUIC transport. On a realistic web workload with variable CPU availability, Pirate achieves 0.63% median measurement error relative to client-side latency. When integrated into the Katran layer-4 load balancer, latency-aware routing cuts 99th percentile latencies by 37%, with only 346 nanoseconds per-packet measurement overhead.

claims.text: Protocol end-to-end latency is dominated by round-trip count, not wire format. Cold-start requirements are: MQTT 3 RTT (pipelined), CoAP unsecured 1 RTT versus 2–3 RTT with DTLS, AMQP 6–8 RTT, and HTTP/3 2 RTT. At 30 ms RTT these translate to 30–240 ms cold latencies. The April 2026 published IoT protocol latency tables were withdrawn by their author due to inability to trace measurements to reproducible sources, making RFC specification-based analysis a more reliable basis for protocol selection than single-rig benchmarks.

claims.text: CoAP's default RFC 7252 retransmission timer (ACK_TIMEOUT 2–3 seconds, doubling on each retry) means a single lost packet incurs 2–3 seconds of latency penalty. This makes CoAP's tail latency worse than MQTT on lossy links despite CoAP's superior p50 latency on clean paths. The protocol specification timer values, not header size or wire format, determine the latency difference between protocols in real-world loss scenarios.

claims.text: Connection migration support is concentrated in specific providers rather than being a universal QUIC capability. Measurements from May 2024 show 52% of QUIC servers with SNI support migration on IPv4, but among IPv6 servers that do support it, 94% are from a single provider (Hostinger), while major providers like Cloudflare and Google do not support connection migration at all. This means an operator's ability to rely on migration for seamless failover depends entirely on which infrastructure vendor is chosen.

meta.capability: You can stop assuming connection migration is available across your infrastructure and start qualifying it as a provider-specific feature that constrains your failover and mobility strategy.

claims.text: SNI creates a 14-fold performance gap in QUIC handshake success (4.9% vs 69% for IPv4 in May 2024 scans), but even with SNI support, only 52% of successful handshakes proceed to migration. Infrastructure that cannot support SNI faces severe handshake failures and cannot rely on connection migration as a recovery mechanism, making investment in QUIC for non-SNI environments economically unjustifiable.

claims.text: TCP throughput is mathematically capped by the bandwidth-delay product formula (Max throughput = TCP_window_size / RTT). A TCP flow with a 64 KB window and 100 ms RTT cannot exceed 5.2 Mbps regardless of physical link bandwidth. Adding network capacity when distance is the bottleneck yields zero user benefit; the fix must address latency, not bandwidth.

meta.query: Above what packet loss percentages or round-trip time values do the measured latency improvements from protocol upgrades become too small to detect or economically justify deployment?
meta.capability: Stop deploying bandwidth upgrades on paths where latency is the bottleneck, and focus on latency reduction instead.

claims.text: Services like Microsoft Teams define acceptable performance targets (RTT < 60 ms, average packet loss < 0.5%, jitter < 3 ms). Operators can rigorously test existing internet connectivity—minimum one week of sampling every 10 minutes, taking the 90th percentile value—against these thresholds to determine if an upgrade like ExpressRoute is economically justified or unnecessary. Internet that meets the thresholds requires no costly alternative; internet that fails them justifies the investment.

claims.text: A network path can show 15 ms latency when idle but 300 ms latency under upload load, due to oversized buffers (bufferbloat) that queue packets instead of dropping them. Testing on quiet links produces false confidence and leads to wasted upgrades; measuring during peak traffic hours reveals the true bottleneck and prevents spending on the wrong fix.

claims.text: Performance thresholds vary significantly across application types, not universally. Voice requires latency under 150ms and jitter under 30ms; video conferencing requires latency under 100ms with jitter under 50ms; general data applications tolerate up to 1000ms latency. This means operators must tailor infrastructure standards to their specific application mix rather than applying a single performance target to the entire network.

claims.text: The first failure point in infrastructure optimization is misidentifying which tier (edge, compute, cache, database, network) actually causes the slowdown. Database teams optimize databases when the edge layer is the bottleneck; network teams reconfigure routing when compute is constrained; compute teams add capacity when an unindexed query is the issue. Starting with incorrect layer selection wastes resources and delays real improvements.
